answer: Yes. The private router (`private.router`, in routes/private.py) is only mounted when `settings.ENVIRONMENT == "local"`. The `ENVIRONMENT` setting in app/core/config.py controls this. The login, users, utils and items routers are always mounted.

Make sure the PR has at least one of these labels: breaking, security, feature, bug, refactor, upgrade, docs, lang-all, internal. The check uses `one_of`, so add exactly one of them. The auto-labeler may add one for you. If it doesn't, add it manually. The check re-runs when you label or unlabel the PR.

Operation IDs come from a custom FastAPI `generate_unique_id_function`, `custom_generate_unique_id`, in backend/app/main.py. It returns `f"{route.tags[0]}-{route.name}"`, which is the route's first tag, a hyphen, then the path function's name (for example `items-read_items`). Every route therefore needs at least one tag, because `route.tags[0]` fails on an untagged route. The frontend generator (frontend/openapi-ts.config.ts) uses these IDs. It groups methods into a `{{name}}Service` class per tag. It also strips the tag/service prefix from each method name and lowercases the first letter, so `items-read_items` becomes `ItemsService.readItems`.

Publishing a GitHub release (release event, type `published`) triggers the "Deploy to Production" workflow. It runs on a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner labelled `production`. The job is skipped in repositories owned by `fastapi`.

The minimum backend test coverage in CI is 90%. The backend workflow runs `coverage report --fail-under=90`, so the job fails if coverage drops below that. The smokeshow workflow also sets a coverage threshold of 90.

A pre-commit hook ("add-release-date") runs `uv run python scripts/add_latest_release_date.py` whenever release-notes.md changes. The script finds the first (latest) header matching `## X.Y.Z`. If that header has no `(…)` date, it rewrites it as `## X.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD)` using today's date from `date.today().isoformat()`. If a date is already there, it leaves the header alone.

A pydantic model validator on Settings (`_enforce_non_default_secrets`) calls `_check_default_secret` for SECRET_KEY, POSTGRES_PASSWORD and FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD. If any of them is still "changethis", it raises a ValueError whenever ENVIRONMENT isn't "local", so the app won't start. In the local environment it only issues a warning.
8 days (ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 60 * 24 * 8 = 11,520 minutes). The login route uses this value as the token's expiry.

Startup fails. Settings validation raises a ValueError ('The value of SECRET_KEY is "changethis", for security, please change it, at least for deployments.') because the environment isn't "local". In local it would only emit a warning. The same check applies to POSTGRES_PASSWORD and FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD.

No. A superuser cannot delete their own account through the users endpoints. DELETE /users/me returns 403 "Super users are not allowed to delete themselves" when current_user.is_superuser is true. DELETE /users/{user_id} returns the same 403 when the target user is the current user (lines 224-227).

The startup script `prestart.sh` runs `backend_pre_start.py`. That script uses tenacity to retry the DB check (`select(1)`) up to 300 attempts (`60 * 5`, about 5 minutes). It waits a fixed 1 second between attempts. The separate compose `pg_isready` healthcheck is a different mechanism: it retries 5 times at 10s intervals.
Backend coverage must be at least 90%. The CI step runs `coverage report --fail-under=90`.

The operationId will be "orders-<function_name>". The function is `custom_generate_unique_id`, which returns f"{route.tags[0]}-{route.name}". `route.name` is the endpoint function's name, so a function named `create_order` gets "orders-create_order". The function is registered as `generate_unique_id_function` on the FastAPI app.

The token is stored in the browser's localStorage under the key "access_token". useAuth.ts sets it after login (line 45), and main.tsx's OpenAPI.TOKEN reads it for each request. When any query or mutation fails with an ApiError of 401 or 403, handleApiError removes "access_token" from localStorage and redirects the browser to /login (window.location.href = "/login").

GET /items/ returns an ItemsPublic object, `{data: [...], count: N}`. A superuser gets every item in the database, and `count` is the total number of items. A normal user gets only the items where `owner_id == current_user.id`, and `count` is the number of their own items. In both cases the items are sorted by `created_at` descending, so the newest come first. Pagination uses `skip` (default 0) and `limit` (default 100). `count` is the total before pagination, not the number of items on the page.

The generated client only includes PrivateService if the OpenAPI schema it was generated from contains the private routes. The backend registers the private router only when settings.ENVIRONMENT == "local". If the client is generated against a non-local backend (staging or production), the private endpoints are absent from the schema, so sdk.gen.ts has no PrivateService and the e2e helper's import fails.
8 days (ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 60 * 24 * 8 = 11,520 minutes)

Run `bash ./scripts/generate-client.sh` from the project root (with the backend virtualenv active), then commit the changes. The script does the following: (1) cd into backend and use `uv run python` to import app.main and dump `app.main.app.openapi()` as JSON to openapi.json; (2) move openapi.json into frontend/; (3) run `bun run --filter frontend generate-client`, which runs `openapi-ts` (@hey-api/openapi-ts, configured in frontend/openapi-ts.config.ts with input ./openapi.json) to regenerate the client in frontend/src/client; (4) run `bun run lint` to format and lint the result. The manual alternative is to download openapi.json from /api/v1/openapi.json into frontend/ and run `bun run generate-client`.

The /admin route's beforeLoad guard fetches the current user (UsersService.readUserMe()) and, if !user.is_superuser, throws a redirect to "/" so non-superusers can't reach the admin page. (The sidebar also only shows the Admin link to superusers, AppSidebar.tsx:23, and the backend enforces superuser too.)

Yes. In corpus/frontend/playwright.config.ts, the `CI` environment variable changes five settings. On CI: `forbidOnly` is on, so a committed `test.only` fails the run (line 17). Retries are 2 instead of 0 (line 19). Workers are limited to 1 instead of Playwright's default (line 21). The reporter is `blob` instead of `html` (line 23). `reuseExistingServer` is false, so the config won't reuse an already-running dev server (line 89). On your machine, with `CI` unset, you get the opposite of each.

An admin (superuser) sees everybody's items, not just their own. The Items page calls GET /items/ (readItems with skip 0, limit 100). For a superuser, `read_items` doesn't filter by owner. Non-superusers only get items where owner_id equals their own id. In both cases the results are ordered by created_at descending, so the newest items come first. They are paginated with skip and limit, and the limit defaults to 100.

Traefik routes `api.${DOMAIN}` to the backend, `dashboard.${DOMAIN}` to the frontend, and `adminer.${DOMAIN}` to Adminer. Each has an HTTP router and an HTTPS router. Traefik's own dashboard is separate, at `traefik.${DOMAIN}`.

Give the runner the label `production`. GitHub also applies the default `self-hosted` label, and the job requires both. The deploy job is triggered by the `release` event with type `published`, which fires when you publish a release. The job is skipped in repositories owned by `fastapi`.

The backend service runs `curl -f http://localhost:8000/api/v1/utils/health-check/` as its healthcheck. It runs every 10s, times out after 5s, and allows 5 retries. I didn't check that the `backend` service key sits above line 85, but the block is in that service's definition, next to its build and Traefik labels.
About 5 minutes: it retries once per second, up to 300 attempts (60*5), before failing.
When CI is set, Playwright uses the 'blob' reporter (so shards can be merged later) and 2 retries. Locally it uses the 'html' reporter and 0 retries.
By default the backend image runs `fastapi run --workers 4 app/main.py`. That starts the FastAPI app in production mode with 4 workers.

The public Traefik gets its certificates from Let's Encrypt through an ACME resolver named "le". It uses the TLS-ALPN challenge (`tlschallenge=true`) and registers with the `EMAIL` variable. Routers opt in with `tls.certresolver=le`. The certificates are stored in `/certificates/acme.json`. That path is on the named Docker volume `traefik-public-certificates`, so they survive container recreation.

Run `docker compose watch`. The frontend is at http://localhost:5173 and the backend API is at http://localhost:8000. Swagger docs are at http://localhost:8000/docs. The same page also lists Adminer at :8080 and the Traefik UI at :8090.

The browser keeps your session as a JWT in localStorage under the key `access_token`. It is saved at login in useAuth.ts and sent as the bearer token on API calls (`OpenAPI.TOKEN` in main.tsx). The kick-out happens in `handleApiError` in main.tsx. Any failed query or mutation that returns an ApiError with status 401 or 403 removes `access_token` and sets `window.location.href = "/login"`. So an expired, invalid or rejected token, or a 403 from any request, sends you back to the login screen. Logging out in useAuth.ts also removes the token.

Open the Mailcatcher web UI at http://localhost:1080. With Docker Compose locally, the backend sends mail to Mailcatcher over SMTP on port 1025. Mailcatcher captures it instead of delivering it, so password recovery emails show up in that web interface.

A password-reset link is valid for 48 hours (EMAIL_RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS = 48). It opens the frontend's /reset-password page, with the token in the query string: {FRONTEND_HOST}/reset-password?token=<token>.

After deploying, open https://dashboard.<DOMAIN> for the web dashboard (the frontend). Open https://api.<DOMAIN> for the API base URL. The interactive API docs are at https://api.<DOMAIN>/docs. <DOMAIN> is the DOMAIN env var you set. For example, with DOMAIN=fastapi-project.example.com the dashboard is https://dashboard.fastapi-project.example.com and the API is https://api.fastapi-project.example.com. Staging adds a staging prefix: dashboard.staging.<domain> and api.staging.<domain>.
docker compose exec backend bash scripts/tests-start.sh   (extra pytest args can be appended, e.g. -x)

The Admin sidebar item only appears for superusers. AppSidebar adds `{ title: "Admin", path: "/admin" }` only when `currentUser?.is_superuser` is true, so your account isn't a superuser. If you go to /admin directly, the route's `beforeLoad` calls `UsersService.readUserMe()`. For a non-superuser it throws `redirect({ to: "/" })`, so you land on the home/dashboard page. The backend also enforces this separately: the user-management endpoints require a superuser (see `backend/app/api/deps.py:53`).

We use Argon2 (via pwdlib; Argon2Hasher is listed first, so it's the default for new hashes). Bcrypt is kept only as a legacy hasher. Accounts with old bcrypt hashes still log in normally. On a successful login, `verify_password` calls `verify_and_update`, which returns a new Argon2 hash. `authenticate` then saves that hash to the user's `hashed_password` in the database. Accounts that never log in keep their bcrypt hash. Argon2 hashes are not rewritten on login.

No. The public `/password-recovery/{email}` endpoint returns the same message whether or not the email is registered ("If that email is registered, we sent a password recovery link"). It only sends the email when the user exists. The `/reset-password/` endpoint also returns the generic "Invalid token" error when the user is missing. The superuser-only `/password-recovery-html-content/{email}` endpoint does return a 404 for unknown users, but it requires superuser access.

Largely no. authenticate() runs verify_password against a dummy Argon2 hash when the email isn't found, so unknown and wrong-password cases take similar time, and the endpoint returns the same "Incorrect email or password" 400 either way. (Minor caveat: legacy bcrypt-hashed users could differ slightly in timing from the Argon2 dummy.)

No, not by default. Sentry is only initialised when SENTRY_DSN is set and ENVIRONMENT is not "local". ENVIRONMENT defaults to "local" (config.py:38), so local runs don't report to Sentry. The exception is a developer who sets ENVIRONMENT to staging or production locally while a DSN is set.

A push (or merge) to the `master` branch triggers the "Deploy to Staging" GitHub Actions workflow. It runs on a self-hosted runner labeled `staging`. It doesn't run in repositories owned by `fastapi`, only in user projects. The job builds the images and starts them with `docker compose up -d`.

Dependabot checks GitHub Actions daily. It checks the uv (Python), bun (frontend), Docker (/backend and /frontend) and Docker Compose ecosystems weekly. The only exclusion is the bun ecosystem, which ignores the `@hey-api/openapi-ts` dependency. No other dependencies are excluded.

The suite is split into 4 parallel shards. The `test-playwright` job uses a matrix with shardIndex 1–4 and shardTotal 4, and fail-fast is off. Each shard runs `docker compose run --rm playwright bunx playwright test ... --shard=N/4` and uploads its own blob report. A `merge-playwright-reports` job then merges the blobs into one HTML report. The tests don't run at all when the `changes` paths-filter job finds no changes in `backend/**`, `frontend/**`, `.env`, `compose*.yml` or the workflow file itself. In that case `test-playwright` is skipped, and the merge job is skipped too, because it has the same condition. The `alls-green` branch-protection job allows that skip. The workflow only triggers on pushes to master, on PRs when opened or synchronized, and on manual dispatch.

The backend lint script runs four checks on `app`. `mypy app` does type checking. `ty check app` does a second type check with ty. `ruff check app` does lint rules. `ruff format app --check` verifies formatting without changing files.

The API accepts cross-origin requests from the origins in the BACKEND_CORS_ORIGINS setting (a comma-separated list of URLs, with trailing slashes stripped), plus FRONTEND_HOST (default http://localhost:5173). The two are combined in `all_cors_origins` and passed to CORSMiddleware as `allow_origins` in main.py.

The session token is not in an httpOnly cookie. It is stored in `localStorage` under the key `access_token`, so any JavaScript on the page can read it. The backend returns it in the login response body, and `useAuth.ts` writes it to `localStorage` after login. The API client reads it back from `localStorage` for each request through `OpenAPI.TOKEN` in `main.tsx`. I found no httpOnly or `set_cookie` usage anywhere in the code. The only `document.cookie` use is the sidebar open/closed state.

It is wiped in two places:
1. **Logout:** `logout()` in `useAuth.ts` calls `localStorage.removeItem("access_token")` and then navigates to `/login`.
2. **API auth failure:** any query or mutation that returns 401 or 403 triggers `handleApiError` in `main.tsx`. That removes the token and redirects to `/login`.

I did not find any other clearing. In particular, the token is not removed on tab close or on a timer. It stays in `localStorage` until one of the two cases above happens. I did not check the backend token expiry setting.

The certificates come from Let's Encrypt. Traefik requests them through its ACME resolver `le`, using the TLS challenge and the `EMAIL` variable. They are not lost when the Traefik container is recreated. The resolver stores them in `/certificates/acme.json`, and that path is on the named volume `traefik-public-certificates`, which outlives the container. A comment in the file says the volume is there "even if the container is recreated". The certificates would only be lost if that volume were deleted.

The user's items are deleted along with the user. In `models.py`, `User.items` is declared with `cascade_delete=True`, and `Item.owner_id` is a foreign key with `ondelete="CASCADE"`. The admin delete endpoint `delete_user` in `users.py` also removes the user's items explicitly with `delete(Item).where(Item.owner_id == user_id)` before it deletes the user. The self-delete endpoint `delete_user_me` only calls `session.delete(current_user)`, so it relies on the cascade. I did not run any of this.

UUIDs. The models define `id: uuid.UUID = Field(default_factory=uuid.uuid4, primary_key=True)`. An Alembic migration converted the old integer IDs to UUIDs. The `User` model has the primary key on this line, and the `Item` model has the same definition at line 88.

It raises an HTTPException with status 403 Forbidden and detail "Could not validate credentials". jwt.decode raises InvalidTokenError for an expired or tampered token, and a payload that fails validation raises ValidationError. The except clause catches both.

If SECRET_KEY isn't set in the environment/.env, Settings falls back to a randomly generated value: `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`. It is a fresh random key on each start, not the "changethis" default that the README describes.

After a successful login, `authenticate` calls `verify_password`, which uses pwdlib's `verify_and_update`. For a bcrypt hash it returns a new Argon2 hash. `authenticate` then overwrites `db_user.hashed_password` with that hash, then adds the user to the session, commits and refreshes it. The bcrypt hash is replaced by Argon2 in the database. If the password is wrong, nothing is updated.

Defaults (config.py): SMTP_TLS=True, SMTP_SSL=False, SMTP_PORT=587, SMTP_HOST/USER/PASSWORD=None, EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL/NAME=None. (compose.override.yml sets SMTP_TLS to "false" for the local setup.) If both SMTP_TLS and SMTP_SSL are true, TLS wins. send_email in utils.py checks `if settings.SMTP_TLS` first and only goes to `elif settings.SMTP_SSL` otherwise, so only tls=True is passed and SSL is ignored.

The `emails_enabled` computed property on the settings decides it. It is true only when both `SMTP_HOST` and `EMAILS_FROM_EMAIL` are set to non-empty values. `send_email` in `backend/app/utils.py` asserts it, and the user-creation route in `users.py` checks it before sending.

Every password field in the request models in backend/app/models.py has min_length=8 and max_length=128. This covers `password` on user create, register and update (optional on update), `current_password` and `new_password` on password change, and `new_password` on password reset. The line cited is one example.

It rejects the request with HTTP 409 Conflict and the detail "User with this email already exists". The handler looks up the new email, and if it belongs to a different user (id differs from the current user), it raises before changing anything. Nothing is saved. Sending your own current email is allowed.

A 403 Forbidden response with the body {"detail": "Not enough permissions"}. GET, PUT and DELETE on /items/{id} all do the same check. If the item doesn't exist, they return 404 "Item not found" instead. Superusers skip the ownership check.

PATCH /users/me/password returns 400 "Incorrect password" if current_password doesn't verify. It returns 400 "New password cannot be the same as the current one" if the new password equals the current one. The CurrentUser dependency can also reject the request (401/403 for bad or missing credentials, 404/400 for a missing or inactive user). Pydantic returns 422 if the body fails UpdatePassword validation, for example when a password length is invalid.

The backend tests use a session-scoped, autouse `db` fixture in `conftest.py`. It opens a Session and calls `init_db`. After the whole test session finishes, it runs `delete(Item)` and then `delete(User)` through that session and commits. There is no per-test rollback or truncation. Cleanup happens once, at the end of the session, and removes every row from the Item and User tables.

No. The /_layout route's `beforeLoad` calls `isLoggedIn()`. If that returns false, it throws a redirect to /login. `isLoggedIn()` only checks that `localStorage` has an `access_token` item (`!== null`). It doesn't check the signature or expiry, and it doesn't ask the server. An expired or bogus token still gets through the route guard. The token is only checked by the backend when API calls are made with it.

The names come from the backend's operationIds plus the SDK plugin settings in openapi-ts.config.ts. FastAPI builds each operationId in `custom_generate_unique_id` (backend/app/main.py:10-11) as `{tags[0]}-{route.name}`. For `read_items` in the router tagged "items", that gives `items-read_items`.

The SDK plugin is configured with `asClass: true` and `operationId: true`. It splits the operationId into a service and a method name. The class name is the tag run through `classNameBuilder: "{{name}}Service"`, so "items" becomes `ItemsService`.

The method name goes through the custom `methodNameBuilder`. This strips the service prefix from the name if it has one, then lowercases the first letter. It is the only step that depends on the operation name starting with the service name.

I didn't trace how the plugin converts `read_items` into `readItems`. The generated `ItemsService` in sdk.gen.ts does have a `readItems` method, so the conversion happens somewhere in the plugin.
If the URL has no token (missing or invalid, which the schema turns into an empty string), the route's beforeLoad redirects to /login. A logged-in user is redirected to / before that check.

The email link is f"{settings.FRONTEND_HOST}/reset-password?token={token}". FRONTEND_HOST defaults to http://localhost:5173, so by default the URL is http://localhost:5173/reset-password?token=<JWT>. The token is valid for EMAIL_RESET_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS, which defaults to 48 hours (2 days).

A first-time visitor gets the "dark" theme. main.tsx wraps the app in <ThemeProvider defaultTheme="dark" storageKey="vite-ui-theme">, which overrides the component's own "system" default. That default only applies when localStorage has no saved value. When the theme is changed, setTheme writes it to the browser's localStorage under the key "vite-ui-theme".

The shared DataTable offers rows-per-page options of 5, 10, 25 and 50. The whole pagination footer is only rendered when `table.getPageCount() > 1`, i.e. when the data spans more than one page. That footer holds the "Showing X to Y of N entries" text, the rows-per-page selector, the "Page X of Y" label, and the first/previous/next/last buttons.

Creating an item (AddItem) invalidates only the ["items"] query key, in onSettled, so it runs on both success and error. Deleting an item (DeleteItem) calls queryClient.invalidateQueries() with no key, also in onSettled. That refreshes every cached query (items, users, currentUser and the rest), not only items.

No. The code branches on `is_superuser`, but both branches give the same tabs. Superusers get `tabsConfig.slice(0, 3)`, and `tabsConfig` has only 3 entries (My profile, Password, Danger zone). Other users get the full `tabsConfig`, which is those same 3 tabs.

A mutation's `onError` is set to `handleError.bind(showErrorToast)`. When the request fails, the generated client throws an `ApiError` that carries the response body. `handleError` calls `extractErrorMessage(err)`, which works as follows:
- If the error is an `AxiosError`, it uses `err.message`.
- Otherwise it reads `err.body.detail`. If `detail` is an array, it uses the first element's `.msg`.
- Otherwise it uses `detail` as is, or "Something went wrong." if there is no `detail`.

`handleError` then calls `this(errorMessage)`, where `this` is `showErrorToast`. That function, from `useCustomToast`, calls sonner's `toast.error("Something went wrong!", { description })`. The extracted message is therefore the toast's description text, shown under the fixed title "Something went wrong!".

UserActionsMenu deliberately returns null when the row's user id matches the logged-in user's id (useAuth().user). This keeps you from editing or deleting your own account from the admin table. Use the user settings page for that instead.

For an admin (superuser), DELETE /api/v1/users/me is rejected with HTTP 403 and detail "Super users are not allowed to delete themselves". The account is not deleted. In the app, the mutation's onError runs handleError, which shows that message in an error toast. The success path (success toast "Your account has been successfully deleted" and logout()) does not run, so the admin stays logged in and the dialog stays open. onSettled still invalidates the "currentUser" query. A normal user would get 200 {"message": "User deleted successfully"}, a success toast, and be logged out.
No. The profile form (UserInformation.tsx) limits full_name to 30 characters with z.string().max(30). The API's UserUpdateMe model in models.py allows 255 (max_length=255).

The `db` service runs `postgres:18`. Its healthcheck runs `pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d ${POSTGRES_DB}` every 10s, with a 10s timeout, 5 retries and a 30s start period. The data is in the named Docker volume `app-db-data`, mounted at `/var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata`, and `PGDATA` points to the same path.

The prestart service uses the backend image and runs `bash scripts/prestart.sh`. That script does three things in order: (1) `python app/backend_pre_start.py` waits for the DB to be up, (2) `alembic upgrade head` runs the migrations, and (3) `python app/initial_data.py` creates the initial data, such as the first superuser.

The backend reports to Sentry in staging and production, but not in local. The init in main.py requires SENTRY_DSN to be set and ENVIRONMENT to not be "local". ENVIRONMENT can only be "local", "staging" or "production", and it defaults to "local". The deploy workflows set it to staging and production and pass SENTRY_DSN from the secrets. Local runs and any run without the DSN stay silent.

The frontend image gets its API URL from the `VITE_API_URL` build arg. In `compose.yml` (production) it is `https://api.${DOMAIN}`, and `DOMAIN` must be set. In `compose.override.yml` (local development) it is `http://localhost:8000`. The override file's `playwright` service, which has its own image, uses `http://backend:8000`.

In nginx.conf, `location /` serves static files from /usr/share/nginx/html with `try_files $uri /index.html =404`. A path that isn't a real file falls back to /index.html, so SPA deep links load the app and the client router takes over. The server block also includes /etc/nginx/extra-conf.d/*.conf. nginx-backend-not-found.conf, which is meant to be mounted there, defines `location /api`, `/docs` and `/redoc`, and each one does `return 404`. So those paths return a plain 404 and never fall back to index.html.
The external Docker network `traefik-public` must exist first. Traefik uses it to talk to your stack(s). Create it on the remote server with `docker network create traefik-public`.

The dashboard is served through Traefik's special `api@internal` service on an HTTPS router for the host `traefik.${DOMAIN}`. The router uses TLS with certificates from the Let's Encrypt resolver `le`. A separate HTTP router for the same host only applies the `https-redirect` middleware, which sends requests to HTTPS with a permanent redirect. The HTTPS router uses the `admin-auth` middleware, which requires HTTP Basic auth with `${USERNAME}` and `${HASHED_PASSWORD}`. The `.yml` file requires both variables to be set. The line cited is the one that attaches the auth middleware to the HTTPS router.

Give the staging runner the label `staging`. The workflow's `runs-on` is `[self-hosted, staging]`, so the runner is a self-hosted one with that label. You can add the label when the runner setup asks for labels, or add it later. A push or merge to the `master` branch triggers the "Deploy to Staging" workflow on it. The workflow is skipped in repositories owned by `fastapi`, so it only runs in your own project. Publishing a release triggers the `production` workflow instead, not this one.

For the backend service, `docker compose watch` syncs the `./backend` directory into `/app/backend` in the container, ignoring `./backend/.venv` and `.venv`. It rebuilds the service when `./backend/pyproject.toml` changes.

compose.override.yml (local stack) publishes these host ports: 80 (Traefik proxy → 80), 8090 (Traefik dashboard → 8080), 5432 (db), 8080 (adminer), 8000 (backend), 1080 (mailcatcher web UI), 1025 (mailcatcher SMTP), 5173 (frontend → container 80), and 9323 (playwright report). compose.traefik.yml separately publishes 80 and 443, but that is the production Traefik setup.

It's a smoke test that the stack builds and starts. On pushes to master and on PRs (opened/synchronize), it runs `docker compose build`, then `down -v` to clean up. Next it runs `docker compose up -d --wait backend frontend adminer`, so those services must start and pass their healthchecks. It then curls the backend health-check endpoint (http://localhost:8000/api/v1/utils/health-check) and the frontend (http://localhost:5173). Finally it tears everything down. It runs no unit tests, and it checks only that the services respond.

No. The unauthenticated POST /private/users/ endpoint (private.router) is only mounted when settings.ENVIRONMENT == "local"; production deploys set ENVIRONMENT=production (deploy-production.yml), so it is not registered/reachable there (unless ENVIRONMENT is misconfigured to "local", which is the default).

In the Test Backend workflow, only the supporting services run in containers. `docker compose up -d db mailcatcher` starts the Postgres database and the mailcatcher mail service. Everything else runs directly on the ubuntu-latest runner. That covers checkout, Python 3.10 and uv setup, the DB migration (`uv run bash scripts/prestart.sh`), the tests (`scripts/tests-start.sh`) and the coverage report (`uv run coverage report --fail-under=90`). The artifact upload also runs on the runner. The backend app and test code are not containerized in this workflow.

Yes. The local dev setup includes the Traefik web UI (dashboard), served at http://localhost:8090. It shows how the proxy is handling routes. compose.override.yml publishes it with port mapping "8090:8080" and enables it with --api.insecure=true.

Yes. Stop the backend container with `docker compose stop backend`. Then run `cd backend` and `fastapi dev app/main.py`. `fastapi dev` reloads on code changes. The Docker services use the same ports as the local dev servers, so the backend is at localhost:8000. Because of that, the rest of the stack keeps working against your local backend.

Install the prek git hook in your local repo. From the `backend` folder, run `uv run prek install -f`. This writes the hook to `.git/hooks/pre-commit`, and `-f` overwrites any existing pre-commit hook. After that, prek checks and formats your code on every `git commit`. If it changes files, stage them again with `git add` and then commit. prek is already a project dependency, and it reads its config from `.pre-commit-config.yaml` at the repo root.

This project uses Alembic. Open a shell in the backend container with `docker compose exec backend bash`. Then generate the migration with `alembic revision --autogenerate -m "Add column last_name to User model"`. Apply it with `alembic upgrade head`. Commit the generated files in `backend/app/alembic/versions`. Alembic is already configured to read your SQLModel models from `backend/app/models.py`.

Edit the local `.env` file and set `DOMAIN=localhost.tiangolo.com`. Then re-run `docker compose watch`. The local Traefik in `compose.override.yml` will route `http://api.localhost.tiangolo.com` to the backend and `http://dashboard.localhost.tiangolo.com` to the frontend. `localhost.tiangolo.com` and all its subdomains resolve to 127.0.0.1, so you don't need to edit /etc/hosts.

Yes. The repo has a ready-made VS Code launch configuration in corpus/.vscode/launch.json. It has two debug configs. The first runs the FastAPI backend under debugpy with uvicorn app.main:app --reload. The second launches Chrome against http://localhost:5173 for the frontend.

Edit the MJML source template `corpus/backend/app/email-templates/src/reset_password.mjml`. It holds the body wording: the heading, the "We've received a request…" text, the button label and the expiry note. The app renders the compiled `reset_password.html` (`build/reset_password.html`, which isn't in this repo snapshot), so recompile the MJML after editing. In the VS Code MJML extension that's the "MJML: Export to HTML" command. The email subject line is separate. It's set in `generate_reset_password_email` in `corpus/backend/app/utils.py`, line 70.

The HTML coverage report is generated by `coverage html` in backend/scripts/test.sh and ends up at /app/backend/htmlcov/index.html in the container. compose.override.yml bind-mounts ./backend/htmlcov to /app/backend/htmlcov, so on the host you can open backend/htmlcov/index.html in a browser. This applies only with the dev override file, and the mount is marked with a TODO to remove it.

Open the Appearance menu (Appearance.tsx) and choose "Light" (it calls setTheme("light"); the other options are Dark and System). Yes, it's remembered: setTheme writes the choice to localStorage under the key "vite-ui-theme", and the ThemeProvider reads it back on load. The default is dark if nothing is stored.

The `prestart` service in compose.yml runs `backend/scripts/prestart.sh` (`command: bash scripts/prestart.sh`). It waits for the DB, then runs `alembic upgrade head`, which creates the tables from the migrations. Finally it runs `python app/initial_data.py`. That calls `init_db` in `app/core/db.py`, which creates the first superuser from `FIRST_SUPERUSER` and `FIRST_SUPERUSER_PASSWORD` if it doesn't already exist. The line cited below is the `alembic upgrade head` step. The admin account is created two lines further down, at line 13 of the same script.

The check (agilepathway/label-checker) requires at least one of these labels: breaking, security, feature, bug, refactor, upgrade, docs, lang-all, internal. Ask for whichever fits your change (e.g. `bug` for a fix, `feature` for new functionality, `docs` for docs).

No. Merging to master only deploys to staging. Production deploys when a release is published (the workflow triggers on `release: published`). It also doesn't run in the main fastapi repo, only in user projects.
